Dear all,

we would welcome a couple more delegates for our workshop on Integrated Population Models (IPM) using BUGS software in Patuxent (30 Oct - 3 Nov 2017). IPMs represent an incredibly powerful framework for using all available data sets on the demography of a population in one single, integrated population model. For virtually all ecologists, BUGS software is currently probably the only way how they can ever learn how to fit IPMs without enrolling the help of a PhD statistician.

Please spread to your friends and colleagues; thanks.

Best regards  ---- Marc

PS: We also still accept applications for the Fairbanks edition of this workshop, which takes place in the week immediately before; see here:  http://www.phidot.org/forum/viewtopic.php?f=8&t=3379&sid=2e4adb7230719b925d6da05ebd2a5936

messages.subject: Re: Calculating WAIC for hierarchical models
messages.body_plain:
See the Gelman paper in the first reply (eq's. 5 and 12).  This paper (http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/waic_stan.pdf) also goes over some additional detail (in Stan, but similar things could be done in JAGS, etc.).

I guess it's worth noting as a general point that despite a lot of the initial optimism regarding WAIC (e.g., the Hooten and Hobbes monograph), follow up work (such as the paper linked to above, Kristin Broms paper on model selection for community models, etc.) should temper expectations.  Just my opinion, but barring taking a thorough out of sample (like, really out of sample) validation approach, it's unclear whether WAIC has better predictive performance than approaches more theoretically similar to BIC/Bayesian Model averaging (variable selection processes, etc.), and the latter don't necessarily require repeatedly fitting models.

messages.body_plain:
In summary, I have a closed population model that I want to estimate (I have a capture history with genotypes (or ID) in rows and capture events in columns). I also have a season matrix (same format as the capture history matrix but containing the seasons in rows for each sampling event).

I constructed the model like this:

    ## Priors ------------------------------------------------------------------
    omega ~ dunif(0, 1)
    for (i in 1:nb.seasons){
      p[i] ~ dunif(0, 1)
    }

    for (i in 1:M){ # M is the number of individuals (or genotypes)
      z[i] ~ dbern(omega)
      for (j in 1:T){ # T is the number of sampling events
        yaug[i,j] ~ dbern(p.eff[i,j])

        # p[season.matrix[i,j]] is the seasonal effect!
        # I created a "season matrix" and I'm sampling from it in
        # order to get the 1:4 p variables
        p.eff[i,j] <- z[i] * p[season.matrix[i,j]]
      } #j
    } #i

    # Derived quantities
    N <- sum(z[])

This is the summary statistics that I get out of the model after the estimation.
Summary of the model:
               mean        2.5%     97.5%  Rhat n.eff
N         31.000000  31.0000000  31.00000 1.000     1
deviance 653.305981 649.7694947 660.64295 1.001  3800
omega      0.969830   0.8922458   0.99915 1.002  1900
p[1]       0.011700   0.0068549   0.01778 1.001  3800 (Fall)
p[2]       0.011843   0.0084588   0.01576 1.002  1300 (Spring)
p[3]       0.002091   0.0004174   0.00494 1.001  2700 (Summer)
p[4]       0.026310   0.0088479   0.05265 1.001  3800 (Winter)

The problem here is that I'm inputting 31 individuals in the capture history and that's exactly the estimate I have out of the model (and the N.effective is 1, which is very bad!).

I was told that this is because I haven't augmented the data properly. I've tried to augment it, but it's not working.

JAGS (which is similar to WinBugs) doesn't recognize NAs in the data that I provide (for convenience, I put the name of the seasons, but in my analysis they are numbers from 1 to 4):
     Seasons
         ch1      ch2
ID1     Fall   Winter
ID2   Summer     Fall
ID3   Winter   Spring
ID4       NA       NA

If you imagine that  ID4 was augmented, the "season matrix", The NAs are not considered:

  3 nodes produced errors; first error: RUNTIME ERROR:
Unable to resolve the following parameters:
season.matrix[32,1] (line 11)
season.matrix[32,2] (line 11)
season.matrix[32,3] (line 11)

So how should I augment the "season matrix"?

Maybe I should not put NAs for the augmented data? Maybe a 5th season? Or just 0s?

The capture history with augmented data looks like this:
         ch1      ch2
ID1        0        1
ID2        1        0
ID3        0        1
ID4        0        0

Thanks for your help again!

messages.subject: RE: Data augmentation
messages.body_plain:
Dear MO,

imagine that your observed data were this (3 individuals is all that you captured over 4 occasions). Then, your data may look like this:

0100
1001
0101

and the covariate X (which specifies the occasion) is this:

1234
1234
1234

Then, augment some animals, say, 2. Response and covariate then look like this:

0100
1001
0101
0000
0000

1234
1234
1234
1234
1234

BTW, I think you don't even need the covariate X. The nice thing about modeling your data in 2 or more-dimensional arrays is that you can use the array dimensions to provide info about covariates such as site, individual or occasion or year. In your case, your model could be written as this:

    for (i in 1:M){ # M is the number of individuals (or genotypes)
      z[i] ~ dbern(omega)
      for (j in 1:T){ # T is the number of sampling events
        yaug[i,j] ~ dbern(p.eff[i,j])

       p.eff[i,j] <- z[i] * p[j]
      } #j
    } #i

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marc-Olivier,

OK, I understand the need for the occasion.matrix as a covariate. So you have 203 occasions then, but they are grouped into 4 seasons, for which you want to estimate separate parameters ?

But is it right to assume that for each individual (= row in the capture-history matrix), the values of the 203 occasions are the same ? In that case, you would simply replicate one line from the occasion matrix for as many additional rows, as you added zero-rows in the caphist matrix.

(If each individual had its own 'sampling regime' ---- not sure how this would happen, but perhaps you would have to tell us more about the design of your study then ---- then I wouldnt really know how to do the DA for the season covariate right now, off the top of my head.)

Regards --- Marc

Cc: beauso...@gmail.com

This would work if I have only 4 occasions, but in my case I have 203 occasions where some seasons are repeated hence the modelling as a matrix. Otherwise, if I had only 4 occasions T = number of seasons and p[j] would be sampled properly. But since p[j] > 4 and that I want the "season" effect I end up with p1, p2 , p3 and p4. If I model p[j], I would have 203 detection probabilities and this would overfit my model or simply, I don't think that this is biologically relevant to model it as having 203 p!

Or maybe there is something that I missed?

But my question is also about the fact that if I add another covariate X (say, temperature...), how do you augment the data with a temperature variable? Do you put random numbers?

Hello,

So we've been on the field collecting feces (non-invasive Mark recapture) and analyzed them to know the individual genotypes. We have collected the feces over 203 days. I regrouped the "days-months" combination into seasons.

Here is an image that will explain what we did.

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-4glQnL2CSLs/WU0Vn2s7fGI/AAAAAAAADNc/yrVTUKGBOlM-s9RTn_AeiBZHSAq7zz7zgCLcBGAs/s1600/Screen%2BShot%2B2017-06-23%2Bat%2B09.20.17.png>

The idea is to see if there is a seasonal effect in the recapture probabilities. But remember here that I'm interested in the estimation of the population abundance. The recapture probabilities would give me an idea of when pandas are more likely to be caught.

As for your comment: "In that case, you would simply replicate one line from the occasion matrix for as many additional rows, as you added zero-rows in the caphist matrix." that's what I finally did and it's working.

Does that make sense?

As for the other problem, I wonder if for example, temperature could affect the recapture probabilities. In this case, I don't know how to deal with the data augmentation.

Marco

Dear Marc,

I think you need to assign a distribution to your missing data. For example:

temperature[i,j] ~ dnorm(mu, tau)

And then have some prior distribution on mu and tau. For example:

mu ~ dnorm(10, 0.001) # here you can use the mean temperature and precision you want

Now you lose me. Isn't it the case that you have a total of 203 occasions on which you tried to detect these beasts ? You detected a total of 31, but you wonder how many more you may have missed on the 203 occasions altogether ? And you also would want to estimate the effects of factors that affect detection probability, such as season and temperature.

So isn't it the case these covariates are constant within one day ? I.e., any one of these 203 days belongs to a particular season and has some particular temperature reading (or for the latter you have to decide on one value, perhaps the mean temp) ? If all of this is true, then you simply take Excel for instance, and copy the values of a covariate within a column as far down as you need to have the same number of rows in your covariate matrix as in your augmented detection history matrix.
